title: How learning slips away - even in the New York Times
author: Martin Skelton
summary: Martin Skelton, writing in his Looking for Learning newsletter, examines the New York Times feature in which 37 experts ranked 30 ideas for fixing US schools. He walks through the Most Effective, Best Value, Worst Value and Worth a Try clusters, adding brief comments on why each reasonable idea is hard to implement well, such as small-group tutoring depending on teachers who understand how learning happens. His central objection is what is missing: none of the top 20 ideas names learning-focused school leadership and management, or a relentless focus on student learning among teachers and stakeholders. He argues this shows how learning is assumed rather than examined, and that evidence based on test scores overlooks how schools actually operate day to day. Drawing on Joe Murphy's finding that the best schools combine consistency with a clear focus on learning, he would flip the list and begin with learning-focused leadership and classrooms. Without those, almost any new initiative risks failing.
points: Skelton's point is not that the NYT experts' ideas are wrong but that each depends on conditions, such as tutors who understand learning, that the ranking leaves unexamined.
None of the 20 ranked ideas addresses developing learning-focused school leadership and management, which sets tone, monitors initiatives and decides how fast a school can take on change.
A focus on learning means looking first at the quality and quantity of student learning rather than teacher performance, and judging initiatives against learning evidence.
Evidence drawn from end-of-year test scores can miss what actually happens in classrooms day to day, which is where initiatives succeed or die.
He would reverse the list and start with learning-focused leadership and learning-focused classrooms, because most other initiatives fail without them.
quotes: Small group tutoring will not work if the tutor/teachers aren’t focused on student learning and aren’t aware of what learning looks like and how it happens. It’s the mediation of small groups by teachers that makes them successful, not small groups themselves.

The science of reading is an overwrought term. There are too many variables in teaching and learning for it to be a science. It would be better to talk about evidence-based methods of improving reading.

I’m not against firing some teachers. I have fired some teachers, almost always on the principle that the children and students they are not helping to learn are more important than keeping a teacher on the staff roll. But it is not easy.

My worry is that many of the people responsible for introducing initiatives aren’t close enough to the day-to-day life of many schools and classrooms and the complex environment new initiatives face. . What makes obvious theoretical sense to them often dies on the battlefield, in education as it does elsewhere.
Not one of the experts’ top 20 ideas mentions the development of high-quality, learning-focused school leadership and management. Isn’t that extraordinary? Isn’t it?
The two key elements of the best schools are high levels of consistency and a clear focus on learning.

It’s another example of how so much of the evidence used to develop and introduce initiatives is based on end of session test scores rather than how schools and classrooms actually operate and what they think they are doing day to day, in real time.
Without both of these being in place, almost every new initiative is in danger of failing.
